_comment: Shared ENT steps: each is used by two or more ENT procedures. Procedure-only steps live in the procedure's steps_local. The shared airway is what makes ENT different from every other specialty, so these steps are mostly about who owns the airway, and when.

step.ent.preop-data-check.title: Confirm the investigation that justifies the operation
step.ent.preop-data-check.why: ENT operations are often elective and sided, and each rests on one investigation: the audiogram and tympanogram for grommets, the CT for sinus surgery, the documented infection count or sleep study for tonsillectomy. Checking it in theatre catches the wrong side, the outdated scan and the indication that has quietly resolved.
how: Display the key investigation in theatre before the time-out, not just in the notes.
Confirm side and indication against it aloud, for example: bilateral effusion with flat tympanograms, or left-sided disease on the CT.
For sinus surgery, the CT stays on screen for the whole operation and is reviewed with the anatomy checklist before the first instrument enters the nose.
If the investigation is missing, outdated or does not support the operation, stop and discuss rather than proceed on memory.
pitfalls: Operating on the side written on the list rather than the side shown by the investigation.
Proceeding on a clinic letter when the scan or audiogram itself has not been seen.

step.ent.airway-share.title: Shared airway plan with the anaesthetist
step.ent.airway-share.why: In ENT surgery the surgeon and the anaesthetist work in the same space. The tube, the throat pack, the gag and the head position all belong to both of them, and an airway plan that is not spoken aloud is an airway plan that only one of them holds.
how: Agree the airway device and its fixation: reinforced or preformed tube, laryngeal mask, or the existing tracheostomy or endotracheal tube.
Agree whether a throat pack is placed, who places it, and record it on the whiteboard so its removal is a counted event.
State the plan if the airway is lost during the case: who acts first, and whether front-of-neck access is the rescue.
For a shared or difficult airway, the surgeon stays in theatre during induction and is ready to act.
pitfalls: A throat pack placed by one person and not recorded anywhere, then left in at extubation.
Assuming the anaesthetist knows how far the head will be extended or turned.

step.ent.pharynx-clearance.title: Clear the pharynx: throat pack out, clot out, postnasal space checked
step.ent.pharynx-clearance.why: A retained throat pack or a clot in the nasopharynx sitting above the larynx can obstruct the airway completely after extubation. This is the ENT version of the swab count, and it is done under direct vision.
how: Remove the throat pack and state its removal aloud so the anaesthetist and scrub practitioner record it.
Suction the oropharynx and, with a mirror or endoscope, the postnasal space. Remove any clot there before it is aspirated at extubation.
Look again at the operative bed with blood pressure restored to normal before declaring haemostasis.
Consider gentle aspiration of the stomach through an orogastric tube when blood has been swallowed, to reduce post-operative vomiting of altered blood that is mistaken for a bleed.
pitfalls: Checking only the oropharynx and missing a clot in the nasopharynx behind the soft palate.
Declaring haemostasis under deliberately lowered blood pressure.

step.ent.airway-handover.title: Airway handover to recovery and the ward
step.ent.airway-handover.why: Most ENT airway catastrophes happen after the operation, in recovery or on the ward, in the hands of people who were not in theatre. The handover is how the theatre knowledge reaches them.
how: State the airway: tube or tracheostomy type and size, whether the cuff is up, whether the upper airway is patent, and whether the patient can be oxygenated from above.
State the bleeding risk and what bleeding would look like: frequent swallowing, fresh blood from mouth or nose, rising heart rate in a child.
For a tracheostomy, confirm the bedhead sign, spare tubes, obturator, suction and humidification are with the patient before they leave theatre.
Position: tonsil position (lateral, head down) after tonsillectomy; head up after sinus and neck surgery.
pitfalls: A handover that covers the operation but not what to do if the airway fails.
A patient arriving on the ward with a new tracheostomy and no emergency equipment at the bedside.

step.ent.bloodless-field.title: Bloodless field: head-up tilt, vasoconstrictor infiltration and the wait
step.ent.bloodless-field.why: Nasal and ear surgery is done through a small opening under magnification, where a few drops of blood hide the plane, the nerve or the flap edge. A dry field is prepared before the incision, not chased with suction afterwards.
how: Ask for a head-up tilt and agree with the anaesthetist on a calm, normotensive or modestly lowered blood pressure and heart rate, using their preferred technique.

Infiltrate local anaesthetic with adrenaline in the correct plane: under the mucoperichondrium for the septum, into the canal skin at four quadrants and the postaural sulcus for the ear. Aspirate before each injection.
Tell the anaesthetist before injecting adrenaline, and check the total local anaesthetic dose against the patient's weight and the agent's maximum.
Wait several minutes after infiltration for vasoconstriction before incising, and use that time to set up the microscope or endoscope.
structuresAtRisk: Canal skin and flaps (blebbing from injection)
pitfalls: Incising immediately after injection, which gives a wet field and wastes the vasoconstrictor.
Injecting too forcefully into the ear canal, which blebs and tears the thin canal skin that forms the tympanomeatal flap.
Not warning the anaesthetist, who then treats an adrenaline-induced tachycardia as light anaesthesia.

step.ent.microscope-setup.title: Operating microscope set-up and surgeon ergonomics
step.ent.microscope-setup.why: Ear and laryngeal surgery is done at high magnification with millimetre margins. A microscope set up badly makes the surgeon lean, lose depth perception and move the patient's head instead of the optics, and every one of those raises the chance of an injury.
how: Choose the objective lens focal length for the operation: a shorter working distance for the ear, a longer one that reaches down the laryngoscope for the larynx. Confirm it before draping.
Balance the microscope, set the interpupillary distance and eyepiece dioptres, and drape it sterile if it will be handled in the field.
Sit with back supported, forearms and wrists rested, and the field at the focal point without stretching. Adjust the table and chair, not your posture.
Connect the camera and recording so the assistant and scrub practitioner can follow, and so findings can be documented.
pitfalls: Starting with the wrong objective lens and discovering it after draping.
Operating with the surgeon's arms unsupported, which turns fine movements into tremor at high magnification.

step.ent.facial-nerve-monitor.title: Facial nerve monitoring: set up, test and agree no paralysis
step.ent.facial-nerve-monitor.why: Facial nerve monitoring helps the surgeon find and follow the nerve, but only if it works. A monitor connected to a paralysed patient or a misplaced electrode is silent, and silence is then mistaken for safety.
how: Agree with the anaesthetist before induction that no further neuromuscular blocking drug is given after intubation, and confirm that any block has worn off before dissection near the nerve.

Place recording electrodes in the facial muscles the system requires, usually orbicularis oculi and orbicularis oris on the operative side, with the ground and return electrodes as the manufacturer specifies.
Check impedances and perform a tap test over the muscles to confirm the monitor responds before the incision.
Set the stimulator current according to the system and your unit's protocol, and keep the face visible under clear drapes so a twitch can also be seen.
Treat the monitor as an aid to anatomical identification, never a replacement for it.
pitfalls: A repeat dose of relaxant given during the case without the surgeon being told.
Assuming the nerve is not near because the monitor is quiet, when the electrodes have come off under the drapes.

step.ent.postaural-exposure.title: Postaural incision, temporalis fascia graft and mastoid cortex exposure
step.ent.postaural-exposure.why: The postaural approach gives a wide view of the mastoid cortex and the posterior canal, and the same incision yields temporalis fascia, the commonest graft for the drum. The bony landmarks exposed here are the map for everything that follows.
how: Incise a few millimetres behind the postauricular sulcus, curving from above the pinna to the mastoid tip. In a young child the mastoid tip is undeveloped and the facial nerve exits superficially, so keep the lower end of the incision high and shallow.

Raise the skin flap in the plane just superficial to the temporalis fascia above, and harvest a generous piece of fascia with a clean, thin layer of areolar tissue removed. Press and dry it for use as a graft.

Make a T-shaped or Palva-type incision in the periosteum and musculoperiosteal layer, then elevate it forwards to the bony canal, exposing the spine of Henle, the suprameatal (Macewen's) triangle, the temporal line and the mastoid tip.
Elevate the posterior canal skin from the bony canal only as far as the operation needs, keeping it intact. Place a self-retaining retractor and check the pinna is not under tension.
structuresAtRisk: Facial nerve at the stylomastoid foramen in young children
pitfalls: Carrying the lower end of the incision deep over an infant's mastoid and dividing the facial nerve where it exits.
Harvesting a thin, holed or small piece of fascia and discovering it is inadequate after the middle ear is open.
Tearing the posterior canal skin while elevating, which then fails to cover the bone and later stenoses.

step.ent.otologic-drill.title: Safe drilling of the temporal bone
step.ent.otologic-drill.why: The drill removes bone a fraction of a millimetre from the facial nerve, the dura, the sigmoid sinus and the inner ear. The rules of drilling are what make it predictable: the injuries come from the wrong burr, the wrong direction, or drilling where you cannot see.
how: Use the largest burr that fits the space. Cutting burrs remove bone quickly on the cortex and in pneumatised air cells; switch to diamond burrs near the facial nerve, dura, sigmoid sinus, semicircular canals and ossicles.
Drill with continuous suction-irrigation to cool the bone and keep the field visible. Heat from a dry diamond burr can injure the facial nerve through intact bone.
Move the burr in long strokes parallel to the important structure, never towards it, and saucerise the edges so the depth of the cavity is always seen from its rim.
Thin bone over a structure until it is identified by colour, as blue over a canal, pink over the facial nerve and dura, rather than drilling until it is exposed.
Before drilling near the ossicles, confirm the burr cannot touch the incus or the chain: drill-to-ossicle contact transmits energy to the inner ear.
pitfalls: Drilling a deep, narrow hole, so the floor of the cavity cannot be seen in relation to the landmarks.
Touching the incus with a spinning burr, which can cause a permanent sensorineural hearing loss.
Running the drill without irrigation for long periods near the nerve.

step.ent.facial-function-check.title: Document facial nerve function before the patient leaves recovery
step.ent.facial-function-check.why: A facial weakness found the next morning cannot be dated: it may be an immediate injury that needs urgent re-exploration, or delayed oedema that usually recovers. Only an examination in recovery, recorded by name and time, tells them apart.
how: Once the patient is awake enough to cooperate, ask them to close the eyes tightly, raise the eyebrows, smile and puff out the cheeks. Compare both sides.
Record the result with a recognised scale such as House-Brackmann, with the time and the examiner's name.
Allow for local anaesthetic infiltration near the nerve, which can cause a temporary weakness for some hours. Re-examine after it should have worn off before drawing conclusions.
An immediate complete palsy that does not recover once local anaesthetic has worn off is discussed with the operating consultant the same day.
structuresAtRisk: Eye (exposure keratopathy if closure is incomplete)
pitfalls: Not examining the face until the ward round, so the onset can no longer be established.
Forgetting eye protection with lubricants and taping when eye closure is incomplete.

step.ent.dental-protection.title: Dentition check and protection
step.ent.dental-protection.why: Gags and laryngoscopes lever against the upper teeth, and dental injury is one of the commonest reasons ENT patients complain. A recorded pre-operative check and a guard prevent most injuries and settle the rest.
how: Check and record loose, crowned, capped and missing teeth, and any loose deciduous teeth in a child, before induction. Include this in the consent discussion.
Place a tooth guard, or folded gauze, over the upper teeth before the instrument goes in.
Lift the gag or laryngoscope along its axis; never use the upper teeth as a fulcrum.
At the end, check the teeth again. A dislodged tooth or fragment is found and removed before extubation, and the event is recorded and explained to the patient.
pitfalls: Levering on the incisors to improve the view in a difficult exposure.
A missing tooth fragment that is not searched for and is later found in the airway.
